digest.intro: Printers in orbit, scans on the seafloor, and a corpus that thinks back.

items.title: Third carrier, 10,000 troops: the US Iran posture hardens
items.blurb: A third carrier group plus fresh troop deployments to the Middle East signals the administration is moving beyond deterrence posture into something closer to strike readiness. The same bulletin notes Ukraine's first combat use of the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile — two simultaneous escalation markers on opposite sides of the world, same day.

items.title: Rodin Museum 3D scan verdict: Cosmo Wenman gets his answer
items.blurb: After years of FOIA-style legal pressure, Wenman's case against the Musée Rodin over withheld 3D scan data of public-domain sculpture has reached a verdict — the outcome sets a precedent for whether cultural institutions can lock digital twins of works the public already owns. For anyone working at the physical/digital boundary this is the access-rights case that actually matters, decided in real time.

items.title: 31 new deep-sea species found without touching a single one
items.blurb: The Schmidt Ocean Institute's latest expedition used DeepPIV laser-based 3D imaging to capture the living cellular structure of midwater organisms — ghostly gossamer worms, comb jellies, and single-celled giants visible to the naked eye — without collecting a specimen. Crucially, the team also imaged a microbe in 3D while it was still alive, a first. Thirty-one new species from the South Atlantic, described entirely through light.

items.title: ESA printed functional metal thrusters in orbit
items.blurb: ESA's metal 3D printer aboard the ISS has now produced and successfully tested thrusters — functional propulsion components made and qualified in microgravity, not shipped from Earth. It's the proof-of-concept moment for in-space manufacturing: the factory follows the mission rather than preceding it.

items.title: Hole Punch: gravity-assist as WebGL toy
items.blurb: A spare, beautifully constrained browser game where you sling a spacecraft around gravitational fields with no fuel — real orbital mechanics, no tutorial, just sector after sector of emergent physics intuition. The HN thread surfaced it alongside Falstad's rendezvous simulator as part of a small cluster of interactive physics tools worth going down.

items.title: Roman's coronagraph sees first light — locked on a dime from 150 miles
items.blurb: NASA's Roman Space Telescope completed its fine-guidance tests September 15–21 and then turned its coronagraph instrument on the cosmos for the first time on September 22nd, capturing stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The pointing stability benchmark: staying locked on a target with precision equivalent to aiming a laser at a dime from 150 miles away. The coronagraph's whole purpose is to blot out a star's glare so we can image what orbits it.

items.title: Your body of work thinks back at you
items.blurb: A photographer realizes he'd been documenting hostile architecture — benches redesigned to prevent sleeping, armrests placed mid-seat, curves that deny rest — without consciously knowing it, one frame at a time over years. The essay's argument: a practice sustained long enough builds an archive that develops its own perception, noticing things the practitioner hasn't yet named. Less about photography than about what any consistent making does to the maker's attention over time.

facts.fact: Roman's fine-guidance system tracks 18 separate guide stars simultaneously — one small section of each of its 18 detectors dedicated to a different reference star — to maintain its extraordinary pointing stability.

The midwater ocean zone — between the sunlit surface and the seafloor — is the largest habitat on Earth, yet the Schmidt expedition found 31 previously unknown species there in a single survey off Brazil.

Ukrainian soldiers wearing Hypershell exoskeletons on the front lines report becoming 'less fatigued, work faster, and maintain combat effectiveness for longer' when carrying artillery shells, according to a colonel cited in Ukrainska Pravda.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film that operates entirely as a feedback loop between image, memory, and meaning — Marker narrates across Tokyo, Guinea-Bissau, and Iceland, treating footage as a system for reconstructing how cultures encode time. Every frame asks what an image is actually doing to the person who made it, and to you watching it now.

art_picks.title: Process Art / Scatter Works (Studio Archive)
art_picks.creator: Robert Morris
art_picks.why: Morris spent the late 1960s making work whose whole point was that the process of making it *was* the piece — gravity, entropy, the behavior of materials. For a builder obsessed with generative systems and expressive surfaces, Morris is the pre-digital ancestor who already understood that constraining a system and watching it run is a valid art practice.

art_picks.title: Tri Repetae
art_picks.creator: Autechre
art_picks.why: The defining record of music as emergent behavior — Booth and Brown build rhythmic systems so complex they feel alive, not composed. The pleasure is architectural: you keep hearing the structure underneath trying to stabilize, and failing beautifully. Made for listening while building something.

events.name: Thomas Ruff: jpegs ny
events.why: Ruff sourced 9/11 images from the internet, then methodically degraded them — increasing compression, dropping pixel density, adding color — until ubiquitous trauma imagery becomes painterly abstraction at the scale of 19th-century history painting; a precise, ruthless investigation of what digital mediation does to collective memory, and it closes Friday.

events.name: Child/ren of the Bloom
events.venue: Pioneer Works, 159 Pioneer Street, Red Hook, Brooklyn
events.why: Digital sensors, holography, and video in Pioneer Works' enormous industrial space — exactly the physical/digital edge Willem builds in, and Pioneer Works remains the best non-institutional venue in New York for work that refuses to sit still in one medium.

events.name: The Surrealist Book: Tomorrow Lives in Mirrors
events.why: The Surrealists treated the book itself as an object to be broken — collage, fold-outs, hidden text, anti-narrative structure — and this show excavates that tradition as a design and systems problem as much as an art-historical one.

events.name: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous
events.venue: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1000 Fifth Avenue
events.why: Reframes two careers not as 'the great man and his wife' but as a genuine feedback loop — how two studios in the same building, competing and collaborating across decades, shaped entirely different but entangled visual languages.

events.name: Jakob Kudsk Steensen: Wetland
events.why: Steensen's Berl-Berl uses game-engine technology and ecological field research to reconstruct Berlin's lost wetlands as a living digital environment — the exact overlap of real-time 3D, environmental systems, and cultural mythology that Willem works in.

trial_sources.name: Global Inequality and More 3.0 — Branko Milanovic
trial_sources.why: A former World Bank lead economist writing sharp, short-form posts on geopolitics, global inequality, capitalism, and the history of economic thought — cited by Adam Tooze, Matthew Klein, and Global Dispatches as essential reading.

trial_sources.name: Ground Truths — Eric Topol
trial_sources.why: A top cardiologist and science journalist offering rigorous, evidence-first reporting on longevity, peptides, stem cells, GLP-1, and AI in medicine — directly matching the reader's health and longevity research interests.

trial_sources.name: Contraptions — Venkatesh Rao
trial_sources.why: Rao's active post-Ribbonfarm Substack explores the aesthetics and feel of technology, organizational theory, status dynamics, and internet culture — the live successor to the archived Ribbonfarm blog the reader already follows.
